reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO & national toxicology guidance
clinicalPearls: Toxicity combines an anticholinergic toxidrome (dry flushed skin, dilated pupils, urinary retention, agitation, delirium) with the far more dangerous cardiovascular and neurological effects
Sodium-channel blockade widens the QRS complex; a broad QRS is the key marker of cardiotoxicity and predicts arrhythmia and seizures
A prominent terminal R wave in lead aVR is a supportive ECG sign of sodium-channel blockade
Life-threatening features include ventricular arrhythmias, hypotension from myocardial depression and vasodilatation, seizures, and rapid deterioration in conscious level
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate is the cornerstone treatment for a widening QRS, ventricular arrhythmia, or hypotension, working by sodium loading and alkalinisation
Deterioration can be abrupt; a patient who looks well early can rapidly progress to coma, seizures, and cardiac arrest, so early cardiac monitoring is essential
Class Ia and Ic antiarrhythmics are contraindicated as they aggravate sodium-channel blockade; refractory arrhythmia may be treated with additional bicarbonate and supportive measures
Intravenous lipid emulsion may be considered as a rescue therapy in refractory cardiovascular collapse
reference.pathophysiology: Tricyclic antidepressants exert several toxic actions. Blockade of fast cardiac sodium channels slows myocardial depolarisation, widening the QRS and predisposing to ventricular arrhythmia and myocardial depression; this effect is worsened by acidosis. Anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) activity produces the classic peripheral and central anticholinergic features. Antagonism of peripheral alpha-adrenergic receptors causes vasodilatation and hypotension, and central effects plus GABA and other receptor actions lower the seizure threshold. Seizures worsen acidosis, which in turn intensifies sodium-channel blockade in a dangerous positive-feedback loop.
additionalDifferentials: Other sodium-channel-blocking drug toxicity (some antiarrhythmics, carbamazepine)
additionalInvestigations: Serial 12-lead ECG focusing on QRS width and the aVR terminal R wave
Arterial blood gas and serum electrolytes including potassium
Capillary glucose and paracetamol/salicylate co-ingestant screen
Creatine kinase if prolonged seizures or immobility raise concern for rhabdomyolysis
redFlags: QRS widening on the ECG indicating significant cardiotoxicity
Seizures or rapidly declining conscious level
Rapid clinical deterioration in a patient who initially appeared stable
reference.prognosis: Most deaths occur early from arrhythmia, refractory hypotension, or seizures, often before or soon after arrival; patients who reach hospital and receive prompt bicarbonate and supportive care and survive the first day generally recover well.
pitfalls: Being reassured by an initially well-appearing patient and delaying continuous cardiac monitoring
Using class Ia or Ic antiarrhythmics, which worsen sodium-channel blockade
Failing to give sodium bicarbonate promptly for a widening QRS or arrhythmia
Allowing acidosis from seizures or hypoventilation to persist and aggravate cardiotoxicity
management: Secure the airway with early intubation for depressed consciousness or seizures, obtain intravenous access and start continuous cardiac monitoring, anticipating abrupt deterioration

Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate as the cornerstone for a widening QRS, ventricular arrhythmia or hypotension, working through sodium loading and serum alkalinisation, and correct hypoxia and acidosis that intensify sodium-channel blockade
Administer activated charcoal for early presentations once the airway is protected
Control seizures with benzodiazepines as first-line agents, avoiding class Ia, Ic and III antiarrhythmics which worsen sodium-channel blockade
Treat hypotension with intravenous crystalloid then a vasopressor such as noradrenaline, and consider intravenous lipid emulsion or extracorporeal life support for refractory cardiotoxicity
Avoid physostigmine and manage hyperthermia and electrolyte disturbance including potassium, checking capillary glucose and a paracetamol and salicylate co-ingestant screen

Observe with cardiac monitoring until the ECG and mental status normalise, then arrange psychiatric assessment and risk evaluation for intentional overdose, with toxicology or poisons-centre and critical-care input
